title: Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics
answer: Polygenic risk, gene editing design, pharmacogenomics, epigenetic age and rare disease diagnosis.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Polygenic Risk Scores
children.blurb: Polygenic risk scores are statistical estimates of an individual's inherited susceptibility to a disease or trait, calculated by summing the small effects of many common genetic variants.

children.name: Gene Editing Guide Design
children.blurb: Gene editing guide design is the computational task of choosing short RNA sequences that direct a CRISPR nuclease to a specific genomic site while avoiding similar sequences elsewhere.

children.name: Pharmacogenomics
children.blurb: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response, including efficacy, dosing, and adverse reactions.

children.name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
children.blurb: Epigenetic aging clocks are computational models that estimate a person's biological age from patterns of DNA methylation, often differing from chronological age.

children.name: Rare Disease Diagnosis
children.blurb: Rare disease diagnosis uses AI to search genomic sequences, clinical notes, and phenotype descriptions for patterns that match known rare conditions.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning to DNA and RNA data to predict disease risk, design gene edits, match drugs to genetic profiles, estimate biological age, and find causes of rare conditions. AI models now score many common variants at once for polygenic risk, propose guide RNA sequences for CRISPR tools, flag gene-drug interactions, train on methylation data to estimate epigenetic age, and rank candidate genes from exome or genome sequences. These are working systems used in research labs, clinical decision support, and some direct-to-consumer reports, not just proofs of concept. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, a portion of which operate in this area. The work is computational and statistical, built on large biobanks, sequencing datasets, and electronic health records.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some tasks are more mature than others. Polygenic risk scores work for a few conditions like heart disease and breast cancer in European ancestry populations, but they transfer poorly across ancestries and explain only part of heritability. Gene editing guide design is good at predicting on-target efficiency in cell lines, yet off-target effects and delivery in living organisms remain hard. Pharmacogenomics has solid evidence for a small set of gene-drug pairs, such as certain HLA and CYP variants, but most drug responses are polygenic and environmental. Epigenetic aging clocks can estimate chronological age from methylation, but their clinical meaning is debated and they can be noisy across tissues and labs. Rare disease diagnosis has seen real progress, with AI ranking candidate variants and matching phenotypes, but many patients still go undiagnosed because the causal variant is noncoding, structural, or absent from databases. No model here is a standalone diagnostic or treatment tool.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for how genetic risk is added up across many small effects would start with Polygenic Risk Scores, which explains the scoring methods and their limits. Gene Editing Guide Design covers the AI that chooses target sites and predicts repair outcomes, and it connects to Pharmacogenomics where the goal is to use a person's genes to adjust drug choice or dose. Epigenetic Aging Clocks sits between risk prediction and diagnosis, showing how methylation patterns are turned into an age estimate that may reflect biological wear. Rare Disease Diagnosis is the most clinically direct page, describing how AI narrows the search for a single causal variant from thousands of candidates. Together these pages move from population-level risk to single-patient explanation, and from prevention to intervention.
